entries.title: Careful affection
entries.body: Pip tried to cuddle up. We had not thought through the spines.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly larva
entries.title: Not hungry
entries.body:
There was nothing wrong with the leaf. Pip had eaten from it. I had eaten from it. A perfectly good leaf.

I put my mouth to the edge and stopped.

Pip brought his head over. I moved away. He came after me, which would once have been comforting and was now enormously annoying.

I climbed to the underside of a stem. He stayed above, chewing. For a while I was glad of the sound. Then I wanted quiet. Then he stopped, and I wanted it back.

I had no useful explanation for any of this.

When he finally went, I was relieved. I was also certain I had been abandoned. I hung there, becoming something, with no improvement at all in my manners.

image.sceneMatch: Large peacock larva on a nettle leaf illustrates the remembered larval body and changing appetite before pupation, not a pictured chrysalis.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly
entries.title: After winter
entries.body: I opened my wings in the sun and stayed there until I could fly. Then I stayed a little longer. The second part was none of survival's business.

image.sceneMatch: Adult peacock holds wings fully open on dry stems in sunshine.

entries.payoff: Necessary warming becomes pleasure once the necessity has passed.

entries.subject: peacock butterfly
entries.title: The other appetite
entries.body: The fly likes this flower too. I tried to imagine tasting it through that face. Lost my place and had to start my sip again.

image.sceneMatch: Adult peacock feeds beside an actual blurry fly on white flowers; fly species and exact sensory anatomy remain unspecified.

entries.subject: Mycena interrupta fungus
entries.title: The leak
entries.body: There is a hole in my cap. The rain gets through. The little thing sheltering underneath has moved to the left. I wish all complaints came with that much initiative.

image.sceneMatch: Blue cap visibly has a missing piece or hole; sheltered visitor is fictional and unpictured.

entries.payoff: The supposed guest solves its problem without demanding impossible repairs from an immobile host.

entries.subject: Mycena interrupta fungus
entries.title: The old weight
entries.body:
The log remembered a bird that used to land on it when it was still a thin branch.

Two feet, a shuffle, then the weight. The whole branch would bend. The bird would stay while the light changed.

I asked how large it had been. The log said enormous.

I looked at my caps. I had been feeling quite expansive that morning. Now I imagined something settling on one of them and bending me right down to the wood.

The log said it had liked the weight. It had missed it when it grew thick enough not to bend.

Later a small brown bird came down beside us. Hopped along the bark. Looked under a loose piece and flew away.

The log said that was the kind.

It was a wren. He had remembered it enormous.

image.sceneMatch: Three small fungi stand on a decaying log. The former tree's remembered birds and later visitor are explicit animistic fiction; no bird or nest is pictured.

entries.subject: Mycena interrupta fungus
entries.title: Blue
entries.body: A drop is sitting on me with a piece of sky inside it. I am keeping very still. This is easy for me. I appreciate a pleasure I am already qualified for.

entries.subject: Mycena interrupta fungus
entries.title: The long pause
entries.body: The wind stopped. My cap took a moment to stop after it. I enjoyed that little bit of wind I was having by myself.

entries.subject: Lycogala slime mold
entries.title: Unevenly
entries.body: The rain touched one side first. I had a cool side and a warm side. For once, being lopsided was giving me something to compare.

image.sceneMatch: Irregular orange Lycogala fruiting bodies on wet wood; imagined temperature sensation, not measured reception.

entries.subject: Lycogala slime mold
entries.title: Everybody at once
entries.body:
There were pink bodies all the way along the log. I could no longer tell who had been there yesterday.

Rain began at the far end. Someone called out. The next one called out too. It came along the wood toward us, voice after voice, although we were still perfectly dry.

I said there was no need to make such a noise about water. The one beside me agreed.

A drop landed squarely on me.

I made a noise I had never made before. Quite a good one. It frightened her.

She asked whether I was hurt. I wasn't. It had been cold and sudden and far more interesting than I had allowed for.

The water was running along the crack now. I could see it coming to her base. I tried to warn her, but she was explaining how much more calmly she intended to take it.

image.sceneMatch: Many orange Lycogala fruiting bodies cover a long split log. Fluid reaching them in sequence is imagined, not a documented field observation.

entries.subject: Lycogala slime mold
entries.title: Over there
entries.body: The small one across the crack is rosy all over. I have spent a lot of time noticing this. She is also round. I am collecting details slowly.

image.sceneMatch: Separated orange fruiting bodies occupy different patches around actual bark cracks.

entries.subject: Lycogala slime mold
entries.title: Rosy
entries.body:
I went gray first.

The one beside me continued being pink in a way I found quite unnecessary. She called me rosy. She meant to be kind. I asked her not to.

The next morning there was a dull patch on her side. I noticed immediately. Managed not to mention it.

By the time the pink had gone, I had been behaving very well for what felt like an enormous portion of my life.

We sat against the damp bark, two gray bodies with very little to conceal from each other.

I called her rosy.

She has asked me not to. I can see why she found it difficult.

image.sceneMatch: Mature gray-brown Lycogala fruiting bodies cluster on damp bark. Sequential color change is a fictional history illustrated by the mature endpoint.
